::: {.eyebrow}
A learning project and a starting scaffold · Graham Watt and Claude Code
:::

These are pieces of music made from real environmental records: river gauges, weather stations, satellites, fish counts, storm tracks and the Keeling curve. Nothing is a simple value-to-pitch beep. Slow signals set the harmony, and faster ones set rhythm, texture and short motifs. Every sound is tagged by whether its data were retrieved, derived or simulated.

This is a first scaffold, not a finished instrument. An interdisciplinary planner brought the questions, the rivers and the domain knowledge. An AI coding agent led the music theory and wrote the code. [How this was made](about.qmd) sets out who did what.

## Pieces

::: {.grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .piece-card}
### [Water Year Rings](water-year.qmd)
One hydrologic year, October 2023 to September 2024, in two southern British Columbia watersheds: the Granby River and the Okanagan. About 7 minutes each, recorded acoustic instruments, with a synced tree-ring page.

[The pieces](water-year.qmd) · [Listen with the visual](listen.qmd) · [Methods](methods.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .piece-card}
### [Climate Pair](climate.qmd)
Sixty-eight years, 1958 to 2025, one year per bar. CO₂, ocean heat, ENSO and a century of storm tracks, heard from the Pacific and from the Atlantic. About 8 minutes each; strings, organ, timpani and synthesizers.

[The pieces and how they work](climate.qmd)
:::
:::

### [Meridian Chorus](meridian/index.html)
Thirteen voices on the 100th meridian, one every 15 degrees from the North Pole to the South Pole, sing one year from the December 2023 solstice to the December 2024 solstice. Each voice sounds while its sun is up, and every voice shares one noon. Air temperature colours the organ, the sea sings on its own floor below, and sea ice quiets it. About 16 minutes in four movements; a 7-minute daylight-only version is kept beside it. A work in progress: the territory acknowledgements for its land voices are still being prepared.

Every track has a card with its version, its records, what drives each sound, what to be careful about, and how to check it byte for byte: see [Tracks](tracks.qmd).

## The code

Everything is open: the data fetching, the instrument engine, the scores and this site. It's all on [GitHub](https://github.com/cordilleran/sonify-viz), under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. Each piece's page lists its data sources and licences.
